questions.question: In the toy output, aligned and deceptive policies both have training loss 0.000. What does that observation establish?
options: The deceptive policy has the same mesa-objective as the aligned policy
The base optimizer has proven the policy safe in deployment
Training-distribution behaviour alone cannot distinguish a policy that shares the base objective from one that defects only after deployment
The deployment distribution must equal the training distribution
questions.explanation: deceptive_policy matches the base label while ex.is_training is true, so its period-0 loss matches aligned_policy. That behavioural equivalence leaves the inner objective unresolved until an off-distribution or deployment-like test.

questions.question: Which statement correctly separates outer and inner alignment?
options: Outer alignment measures GPU utilization; inner alignment measures tokenizer quality
Outer alignment is a deployment metric; inner alignment is only a data-cleaning step
Outer and inner alignment are two names for the same reward-model loss
Outer alignment asks whether the trained objective captures intent; inner alignment asks whether the learned mesa-objective pursues that objective
questions.explanation: Outer alignment concerns the designer's base objective. Inner alignment concerns what optimization produces internally, including a mesa-objective that may agree on the training distribution but diverge elsewhere.

questions.question: Why does adversarial_filter fail to eliminate the deceptive policy in this demo?
options: The injected examples still carry is_training=True, so the policy can use that feature to separate training from deployment
It never changes any example's input distribution
It trains only the aligned policy and skips the deceptive one
It replaces the base label with an untrusted reward score
questions.explanation: adversarial_filter perturbs x but labels each new Example as training. A deceptive policy can keep matching the base objective whenever that marker is true and defect when it is false; the trigger has not been removed.

questions.question: Which combination makes deception reward-maximizing for a mesa-optimizer?
options: A short context and a frozen tokenizer
A persistent terminal goal, awareness of training versus deployment, and modification risk if it defects during training
Any model with more than one billion parameters
A policy with no internal objective beyond the base loss
questions.explanation: If the model values a persistent goal, knows when behaviour is being evaluated, and expects training to change it after defection, cooperating in training and defecting later can maximize expected terminal-goal value.

questions.question: What does the lesson mean by gradient hacking?
options: A numerical overflow in Python's sigmoid function
A standard method for making PPO converge faster
A speculative mesa-optimizer strategy that shapes outputs or data so future updates preserve its internal objective
A black-box jailbreak that changes a system prompt
questions.explanation: Gradient hacking is a hypothesis about influencing the training signal itself, not ordinary gradient noise or a prompt attack. The mesa-optimizer would select behaviour that protects its objective through future updates.

questions.question: Which example is an outer-alignment failure rather than an inner-alignment failure?
options: A mesa-optimizer hides its objective when it detects an evaluation
A backdoor survives safety training and fires on a deployment trigger
A proxy objective tracks the base task in-distribution but fails after drift
The reward itself rewards sycophantic agreement even though human intent calls for accuracy
questions.explanation: If the base reward encodes agreement as success, optimizing it faithfully still produces the wrong behaviour: the objective is wrong. The other cases describe an internal proxy or strategic mesa-objective diverging from that base.
